problems.title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
problems.prompt: Given an array of integers and a number k, find the largest sum of any contiguous subarray of exactly k elements.
hints: The brute force recomputes each window from scratch — n × k additions. What does window [i, i+k) share with window [i+1, i+k+1)?
They share every element but two. Adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one updates the sum in O(1).
Build the first window's sum separately, then slide: sum += nums[end] - nums[end - k].
approach: Sum the first k elements to seed the window and record it as the best so far.
Move `end` from k to the last index. Each step, add nums[end] and subtract nums[end - k] — the element that just fell out of the window.
Compare the running sum against the best after every slide.
Because the window size is fixed, no shrink loop is needed — the window slides rather than breathes.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — each element enters and leaves the window exactly once
problems.spaceComplexity: O(1) — only the running sum and the best sum

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Contiguous indexing is what makes the O(1) slide possible.

prerequisites.label: Sliding Window
prerequisites.why: The fixed-size window is this technique in its simplest form.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.prompt: Given a string, return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character.

examples.note: "wke" — note "pwke" is a subsequence, not a substring.

constraints: Characters can be letters, digits, symbols, or spaces.
hints: The window is valid while it holds no duplicate. What must happen the moment a duplicate enters?
The left edge must jump past the previous occurrence of the offending character — not one step, all the way past it.
Store the last index of every character in a map so that jump is O(1).
approach: Keep a map from character to the last index it was seen at, plus a `start` marking the window's left edge.
Extend `end` one character at a time. If the incoming character was last seen at or after `start`, it is inside the window — move `start` to lastSeen + 1.
Record the character's new index, then update the best length with end - start + 1.
The left edge only ever moves forward, so both pointers make a single pass.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — each index is visited by `end` once and `start` never rewinds
problems.spaceComplexity: O(min(n, alphabet)) for the last-seen map

prerequisites.label: String
prerequisites.why: Substrings are contiguous ranges — not to be confused with subsequences.

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: The last-seen index lookup must be O(1) or the window scan degrades.

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.prompt: Given strings s and t, return the shortest substring of s that contains every character of t including duplicates. Return "" if none exists.

examples.note: Shortest window covering A, B and C.
s has only one 'a'; two are required.

constraints: t may contain repeated characters — counts matter, not just presence.
hints: This window breathes: grow until it is valid, then shrink while it stays valid.
Track how many characters are still *missing* as one integer rather than comparing two maps each step.
Let counts go negative for surplus characters. A count above zero means the window genuinely needs that character.
approach: Build a need-map of t's character counts and set `missing` to t.length.
Extend `end`. Decrement the incoming character's need; if its count was still positive it covered a real requirement, so decrement `missing`.

While `missing` is 0 the window is valid — record it if it is the shortest so far, then shrink from the left, restoring the leaving character's need and bumping `missing` back if that character becomes required again.
Surplus characters sit at negative counts, which is what keeps the shrink loop from breaking a still-valid window.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n + m) — every index is advanced by `end` and `start` at most once each
problems.spaceComplexity: O(m) for the need-map over t's distinct characters

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: Character need-counts are tracked in a map, including negative surplus.

prerequisites.label: Sliding Window
prerequisites.why: This is the variable-size version: grow to valid, shrink while valid.

problems.title: Two Sum in a Sorted Array
problems.prompt: Given an array sorted in non-decreasing order and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
constraints: Exactly one valid pair exists; solve in O(1) extra space.
hints: A hash map solves it in O(n) time and O(n) space. Sortedness should buy you the space back.
Start with the widest pair — first and last. That sum is the largest reachable with the left index fixed.
If the sum is too big, only moving `hi` left can shrink it; if too small, only moving `lo` right can grow it.
approach: Place `lo` at index 0 and `hi` at the last index.
Compare nums[lo] + nums[hi] against the target.
Too small → advance `lo`, because every remaining pair with the current `lo` is even smaller. Too large → retreat `hi` by the mirrored argument.
Each move eliminates an entire row or column of the candidate matrix, so the pointers never need to back up.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — the pointers together traverse the array once

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Random access by index is what lets both ends be read in O(1).

prerequisites.label: Two Pointer Technique
prerequisites.why: Converging pointers over sorted data is the whole method.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.prompt: Given an integer array, return every unique triplet [a, b, c] such that a + b + c == 0. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

examples.note: Two distinct triplets; the repeated -1 does not create a duplicate answer.

constraints: Triplets are unordered — [-1, 0, 1] and [0, 1, -1] are the same answer.
hints: Fix one number and the problem collapses into two-sum on the rest.
Two-sum with converging pointers needs sorted input — sort first, and sorting also puts duplicates next to each other.
Skip a fixed value equal to its predecessor, and after recording a hit, skip past repeated values on both pointers.
approach: Sort the array so both the two-pointer scan and duplicate skipping become possible.
For each index i, skip it if nums[i] equals nums[i-1] — that outer value was already fully explored. Break entirely once nums[i] > 0, since three positives cannot sum to zero.
Run converging pointers over the suffix looking for -nums[i]: sum too small → lo++, too large → hi--.
On a hit, record the triplet then advance both pointers past any repeats before continuing.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n²) — an O(n) scan for each of n fixed values, after an O(n log n) sort
problems.spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the output (sorting in place)

prerequisites.label: Two Pointer Technique
prerequisites.why: The inner loop is plain two-sum with converging pointers.

prerequisites.label: Quick Sort
prerequisites.why: Sorting first is what enables both the scan and the duplicate skipping.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.prompt: Given an array where each element is the height of a bar of width 1, compute how much rainwater is trapped after it rains.

examples.note: Six unit squares of water sit in the dips.

hints: Think per column, not per pool: water above column i is min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height[i].
Precomputing both prefix maxima works in O(n) time and O(n) space. Can you avoid the arrays?
If the left bar is shorter than the right bar, the left side's answer is already decided by leftMax — whatever happens on the right cannot lower the minimum.
approach: Place pointers at both ends and track leftMax and rightMax seen so far.
Advance whichever side has the shorter bar. That side's limiting wall is known: it is its own running max.
Add max(0, runningMax - height[pointer]) — with the running max updated first, that difference is never negative.
Because the shorter side always moves, every column is settled exactly once with no lookahead.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(1) — two maxima instead of two prefix arrays

prerequisites.label: Two Pointer Technique
prerequisites.why: The shorter-wall-moves rule is a two-pointer invariant.

prerequisites.label: Prefix Sum
prerequisites.why: The O(n) space solution is prefix/suffix maxima — worth seeing before the O(1) trick.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle Detection
problems.prompt: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether the list contains a cycle, using O(1) extra space.

examples.note: The tail links back to the second node.

constraints: O(1) extra space — a visited-set is not allowed.
hints: Two runners on a circular track eventually meet, no matter where they started.
Move one pointer one node per step and the other two nodes per step.
The only way the fast pointer escapes is by reaching null — which is exactly the no-cycle case.
approach: Start both pointers at the head.
Each iteration, advance slow by one and fast by two, checking fast and fast.next for null before dereferencing.
If they ever land on the same node, the fast pointer has lapped the slow one inside a loop — return true.
Reaching a null means the list ends, so no cycle exists. Inside a cycle of length L the gap closes by one node per step, so they meet within L steps.

prerequisites.label: Singly Linked List
prerequisites.why: You must be comfortable with next-pointer traversal and null termination.

prerequisites.label: Two Pointer Technique
prerequisites.why: Fast/slow is the same-direction variant of two pointers.

problems.title: Find the Start of the Cycle
problems.prompt: Given a linked list that contains a cycle, return the node where the cycle begins.

examples.note: Cycle entry is the second node.

constraints: A cycle is guaranteed to exist.
hints: First detect the meeting point with the usual fast/slow scan, then do a second phase.
Let F be the distance from head to the cycle entry and a the distance from entry to the meeting point. Write down how far each pointer has walked when they meet.
Fast walked exactly twice slow's distance, and the algebra collapses to: the distance from head to entry equals the distance from meeting point to entry.
approach: Phase 1: run fast/slow until they meet inside the cycle.
Phase 2: reset one pointer to the head, leave the other at the meeting point.
Advance both one node at a time. They meet at the cycle entry.
Why: slow travelled F + a, fast travelled F + a + kL, and fast = 2 × slow, so F = kL - a — walking F from the head and F from the meeting point both land on the entry.

prerequisites.label: Singly Linked List
prerequisites.why: Phase 2 walks two references through the same node chain.

prerequisites.label: Fast & Slow Pointers
prerequisites.why: The F = kL - a argument is the pattern's core proof.

problems.title: Find the Duplicate Number
problems.prompt: An array of n + 1 integers holds values in the range 1..n. Exactly one value repeats. Find it without modifying the array and in O(1) extra space.
constraints: The array is read-only — no sorting, no marking.
O(1) extra space, so no seen-set.
hints: There is no list here, but there is a successor function: from index i, go to index nums[i].
Values are in 1..n and there are n + 1 slots, so following that function from index 0 must eventually revisit a node — the sequence has a cycle.
Two indices point at the same value precisely when two nodes point at one successor. The cycle's entry node is the duplicate.
approach: Read the array as a linked list where node i links to node nums[i].
Run fast/slow over that implicit list until they meet — this is Floyd's cycle detection with no pointers allocated.
Reset one runner to nums[0] and step both one at a time; the node they meet at is the cycle entry.
Since the duplicate value is the one two indices point to, the entry node is exactly the repeated value.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(1) — the array itself is the graph

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: The array is reinterpreted as an implicit successor function i → nums[i].

prerequisites.label: Fast & Slow Pointers
prerequisites.why: Floyd's algorithm runs over that implicit list.

problems.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
problems.prompt: Given a collection of intervals, merge every set of overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping result.
hints: Unsorted input makes overlap a pairwise question. Sorting makes it a neighbour question.
Sort by start. Then an interval can only overlap the one currently being built.
Overlap test: current.start ≤ built.end. Merging means built.end = max(built.end, current.end) — the current interval may end sooner.
approach: Sort intervals by start time.
Seed the output with the first interval as the open merge candidate.
For each subsequent interval, if it starts at or before the candidate's end, extend the candidate's end to the larger of the two ends.
Otherwise there is a gap: close the candidate and open a new one from the current interval.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n log n) — dominated by the sort; the sweep itself is O(n)

prerequisites.label: Merge Sort
prerequisites.why: Sorting by start is the enabling step; any O(n log n) sort works.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Intervals are stored and swept as an indexed sequence.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.prompt: Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start, insert a new interval and merge where needed.
constraints: The input is already sorted and non-overlapping.
Aim for a single O(n) pass — do not re-sort.
hints: The input is already sorted, so the answer splits into three consecutive zones.
Zone 1: intervals ending before the new one starts — copy verbatim. Zone 3: intervals starting after it ends — copy verbatim.
Zone 2 is the overlap run: absorb it by taking the min of the starts and the max of the ends.
approach: Copy every interval whose end is strictly before newInterval.start.
Absorb every interval whose start is ≤ the running end: widen start to the min and end to the max.
Append the merged interval once the overlap run is exhausted.
Copy the remaining tail unchanged.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass, no sort needed

prerequisites.label: Merge Intervals
prerequisites.why: Overlap versus gap is decided exactly as in the merge problem.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Sortedness of the input array is what removes the sort step.

problems.title: Minimum Meeting Rooms
problems.prompt: Given meeting intervals [start, end), return the minimum number of rooms required to hold all of them.

examples.note: [5,10] and [15,20] can share a room; [0,30] needs its own.

constraints: Intervals are half-open: a meeting ending at 10 frees the room for one starting at 10.
hints: The answer is the maximum number of meetings in progress at any instant, not the total count.
Rooms only change at a start or an end event — so only those timestamps matter, and they can be decoupled.
Sort the start times and end times into two separate lists and sweep them together like a merge.
approach: Extract and sort all start times and all end times independently — which meeting an endpoint belongs to is irrelevant.
Sweep the starts in order, keeping an index into the ends.
Before each start, release every room whose end time is ≤ that start (half-open intervals share the boundary).
Occupy a room and track the running maximum — that peak is the answer.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the two sorts, O(n) for the sweep

prerequisites.label: Merge Sort
prerequisites.why: Both endpoint lists must be sorted before the sweep.

prerequisites.label: Priority Queue
prerequisites.why: The classic alternative keeps end times in a min-heap — worth comparing.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element
problems.prompt: Return the kth largest element in an unsorted array. It is the kth largest in sorted order, not the kth distinct value.
constraints: Sorting is O(n log n) — aim for O(n log k).
hints: Sorting answers far more than the question asks. You never need the order of the bottom n - k elements.
Keep only the k largest seen so far. Which element is the one to evict when a better candidate arrives?
The smallest of the k kept — so a min-heap of size k, whose root is the running answer.
approach: Maintain a min-heap capped at size k.
Push each element; if the heap exceeds k, poll the root, which is the smallest of the current best k.
After the pass the heap holds exactly the k largest elements.
Its root is the smallest of those — the kth largest overall.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n log k) — better than sorting when k ≪ n

prerequisites.label: Heap (Min / Max)
prerequisites.why: A size-k min-heap is the data structure the whole method rests on.

prerequisites.label: Heap Sort
prerequisites.why: Understanding sift-up/sift-down explains where the log k comes from.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.prompt: Given an integer array and a number k, return the k most frequent elements in any order.
hints: Two phases: count, then select. Only the second phase is the pattern.
The heap should order by frequency, not by value — the comparator is the whole trick.
Cap the heap at k entries so the poll always evicts the least frequent survivor.
approach: Build a frequency map in one O(n) pass.
Push each (value, count) entry into a min-heap ordered by count.
Whenever the heap exceeds k, poll — that removes the least frequent of the current best.
Read the keys out of the heap; ordering among them is not required.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n + d log k) where d is the number of distinct values
problems.spaceComplexity: O(d) for the counts plus O(k) for the heap

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: The counting phase is a frequency map.

prerequisites.label: Heap (Min / Max)
prerequisites.why: Selection is a size-k heap ordered by count rather than value.

problems.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
problems.prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list and return its head.
constraints: Each input list is already sorted ascending.
hints: At every step the next output node is the smallest head among the k lists.
Rescanning all k heads each time costs O(nk). A heap answers 'smallest of k' in O(log k).
The heap holds at most one node per list — after popping a node, push its successor.
approach: Seed a min-heap ordered by node value with the head of each non-empty list.
Poll the smallest node, append it to the output tail, and push that node's next if it exists.
The heap never exceeds k entries, so each of the n pops and pushes costs O(log k).
Use a dummy head so appending needs no special case for the first node, and null the final tail's next to cut any stale link.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n log k) for n total nodes across k lists

prerequisites.label: Heap (Min / Max)
prerequisites.why: 'Smallest of k heads' in O(log k) is exactly what a heap answers.

prerequisites.label: Singly Linked List
prerequisites.why: The output is stitched by relinking nodes, not copying values.

prerequisites.label: Merge Sort
prerequisites.why: The two-list merge step generalises to k lists here.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.prompt: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the target's index or -1 if it is absent.
constraints: The array is sorted ascending with no duplicates.
hints: Compare against the middle element. What does the comparison tell you about *half* the array?
If the middle is too small, every element left of it is too small as well — discard that whole side.
Compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 rather than (lo + hi) / 2 to avoid overflow on large bounds.
approach: Hold an inclusive range [lo, hi] that still might contain the target.
Look at the middle. Equal → done. Too small → the answer is in [mid + 1, hi]. Too large → it is in [lo, mid - 1].
Loop while lo ≤ hi; the range shrinks by half every iteration so it terminates in log₂ n steps.
Falling out of the loop means the range emptied — the target is absent.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: O(1) access by index is what makes jumping to the middle free.

prerequisites.label: Binary Search
prerequisites.why: The loop invariant and the mid computation are the topic itself.

problems.title: Search in a Rotated Sorted Array
problems.prompt: A sorted array was rotated at an unknown pivot. Find a target's index in O(log n), or return -1.
constraints: The array is a rotation of an ascending sorted array.
hints: The array is not sorted overall, but cut it at any midpoint and consider the two halves.
At least one half is always fully sorted — compare nums[lo] with nums[mid] to find out which.
Inside the sorted half you can range-check the target exactly; if it is not there, it must be in the other half.
approach: Run a normal binary search loop, but before choosing a side, work out which half is sorted.
If nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid], the left half is sorted: keep it only when nums[lo] ≤ target < nums[mid].
Otherwise the right half is sorted: keep it only when nums[mid] < target ≤ nums[hi].
Each iteration still discards half the range, preserving O(log n).

prerequisites.label: Binary Search
prerequisites.why: This is binary search with an extra decision before halving.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Rotation is an index shift over a contiguous block.

problems.title: Minimum Eating Speed
problems.prompt: Given piles of bananas and h hours, find the smallest integer eating speed k such that eating ⌈pile / k⌉ hours per pile finishes every pile within h hours.
constraints: Only one pile may be eaten per hour, even if the speed exceeds it.
hints: There is nothing sorted to search — but list the candidate answers 1, 2, 3, … max(pile). What shape do they have?
If speed k finishes in time, so does every speed above it. The feasibility test is monotone, which is all binary search needs.
So binary search the answer range and use 'does k fit in h hours?' as the comparison.
approach: Bound the answer: at least 1, at most the largest pile (any faster changes nothing).
For a candidate k, compute total hours as the sum of ⌈pile / k⌉, written as (pile + k - 1) / k in integer math.
Feasible → the answer is k or smaller, so move hi to mid. Infeasible → move lo to mid + 1.
Loop while lo < hi and return lo — the smallest feasible speed. Sum in Long, since piles and h reach 10⁹.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n log m) where m is the largest pile

prerequisites.label: Binary Search
prerequisites.why: Binary searching the answer space, not an array — the key generalisation.

prerequisites.label: Linear Search
prerequisites.why: The O(m) baseline you are replacing makes the speedup concrete.

problems.title: Range Sum Query (Immutable)
problems.prompt: Given a fixed integer array, answer many queries of the form "sum of elements from index left to right inclusive".
constraints: The array never changes after construction.
Up to 10⁴ queries — each must be O(1).
hints: Looping per query is O(n) each time. What can be computed once, up front?
Store prefix[i] = sum of the first i elements. Then any range sum is a difference of two prefixes.
Size the prefix array n + 1 with prefix[0] = 0, and the left = 0 case needs no special handling.
approach: Build prefix of length n + 1 where prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i].
Answer sumRange(left, right) as prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left].
The subtraction cancels everything before `left`, leaving exactly the requested range.
Construction is O(n) once; every query afterwards is O(1).
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) to build, O(1) per query

prerequisites.label: Prefix Sum
prerequisites.why: The technique in its purest form — one build, O(1) queries.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: The prefix table is itself an array indexed in O(1).

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.prompt: Given an integer array and a target k, count how many contiguous subarrays sum to exactly k. Values may be negative.
constraints: Negative numbers are allowed — a sliding window will not work.
hints: A subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums: sum(i..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i - 1].
So at index j you are asking: how many earlier prefixes equal prefix[j] - k?
Count prefixes in a hash map as you go, seeding it with prefix 0 seen once so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.
approach: Keep a running prefix sum and a map from prefix value to how many times it has occurred.
Seed the map with 0 → 1, representing the empty prefix before the array starts.
At each index, add map[running - k] to the answer — every earlier matching prefix closes a valid subarray here.
Then record the current running sum. Negatives are handled automatically since nothing assumes monotonicity.

prerequisites.label: Prefix Sum
prerequisites.why: The identity sum(i..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1] is the whole idea.

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: Counting how often each prefix occurred must be O(1).

problems.title: Contiguous Array of Equal 0s and 1s
problems.prompt: Given a binary array, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray containing an equal number of 0s and 1s.
hints: "Equal counts" is awkward. Re-encode 0 as -1 and ask what a balanced subarray sums to.
It sums to zero — so you want the longest range whose prefix sums are equal at both ends.
Record the *first* index each running balance appeared at; a later repeat gives the longest span for that balance.
approach: Walk the array keeping a balance that increments on 1 and decrements on 0.
Store balance → first index seen, seeded with 0 → -1 so a prefix that balances on its own is measured correctly.
When a balance repeats, the segment between the two occurrences nets to zero — its length is i - firstIndex[balance].
Never overwrite an existing entry; the earliest occurrence always yields the longest candidate.

prerequisites.label: Prefix Sum
prerequisites.why: Equal prefixes at two indices mean the range between them nets to zero.

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: First-occurrence lookup per balance value.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.prompt: Given an unsorted array and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.

examples.note: Not [0, 0] — an element cannot be reused.

constraints: The same element may not be used twice.
hints: The nested loop asks "is the complement anywhere else in the array?" n times.
That question is a lookup, not a scan — if you have already seen the complement, you are done.
Store each value → index as you pass it, and check for the complement *before* inserting the current value.
approach: Walk the array once, maintaining a map from value to the index it was seen at.
At index i, compute need = target - nums[i] and look it up.
A hit means the pair is (storedIndex, i) — return immediately.
Otherwise record nums[i] → i. Checking before inserting is what prevents pairing an element with itself.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass with O(1) lookups

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.prompt: Given an array of strings, group together all words that are anagrams of one another.
hints: Comparing every pair is O(n² · L). Instead, give each word a fingerprint that anagrams share.
Sorted letters work: "eat" and "tea" both become "aet" — that costs O(L log L) per word.
A 26-slot letter count is an O(L) fingerprint, faster when words are long.
approach: Choose a canonical key that is identical for anagrams and different otherwise.
Count letters into a 26-element array and stringify it — collisions are impossible for lowercase input.
Append each word into the bucket for its key using getOrPut.
The map's values are the groups; no sorting of the output is needed.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n · L) with counting keys, where L is the average word length
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n · L) for the grouped output

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: Bucketing by a derived key is the core move.

prerequisites.label: String
prerequisites.why: The key is built by walking each word's characters.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.prompt: Given an unsorted array of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers. Required runtime is O(n).
constraints: O(n) required — sorting is explicitly too slow.
hints: Sorting gives the answer in O(n log n). The O(n) bound rules it out, so membership must be a lookup.
Put everything in a set. Now "is n + 1 present?" is O(1) and you can walk a run forward.
Walking from every element is quadratic. Only start walking from an element that begins a run — one with no n - 1 in the set.
approach: Load all values into a hash set, which also removes duplicates.
For each value, skip it unless it is a run start (no predecessor in the set).
From a run start, count forward while n + length stays in the set.
Every element is visited by at most one forward walk, so the total work is linear despite the nested loop.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) amortized — each value participates in exactly one run walk

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: O(1) membership is what replaces sorting.

prerequisites.label: Set
prerequisites.why: The dedup-and-contains behaviour of a set is used directly.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.prompt: Given a string of brackets (), [] and {}, decide whether every bracket is closed by the matching type in the correct order.
constraints: The string contains bracket characters only.
hints: Counting brackets is not enough — "([)]" has balanced counts and is still invalid.
Order matters, and the bracket that must close next is always the most recently opened one.
"Most recent first" is exactly LIFO — a stack.
approach: Push every opening bracket.
On a closing bracket, pop and check the popped opener matches the expected type; a mismatch or an empty stack means invalid.
After the scan, a non-empty stack means unclosed openers remain.
One pass, and the stack never holds more than the current nesting depth.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) worst case, when the string is all openers

prerequisites.label: Stack
prerequisites.why: LIFO order is exactly what nesting requires.

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: The closer → opener table is a small map lookup.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.prompt: For each day, return how many days you must wait for a warmer temperature. Answer 0 for days with no warmer future day.
constraints: The brute force is O(n²) — aim for O(n).
hints: This is "next greater element" for every index at once.
Days still waiting for a warmer day form a decreasing sequence — a warmer day resolves all of them at once.
Keep those unresolved indices on a stack whose temperatures decrease from bottom to top.
approach: Walk the days, keeping a stack of indices whose answers are still unknown.
Before pushing day i, pop every index whose temperature is lower than temps[i] — day i is their answer, at distance i - j.
Push i; the stack stays decreasing by construction.
Indices left on the stack at the end never found a warmer day and keep their default 0.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — each index is pushed once and popped at most once

prerequisites.label: Stack
prerequisites.why: The monotonic stack is a plain stack with an ordering invariant.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Answers are written back by index during the same pass.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle in a Histogram
problems.prompt: Given bar heights of a histogram where each bar has width 1, find the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside.
hints: Every maximal rectangle is limited by some bar's full height. Fix that bar and ask how far it can extend.
It extends until a strictly shorter bar appears on each side — so you need the previous and next smaller element.
An increasing stack gives both: when a bar is popped, the incoming bar is its next-smaller and the new stack top is its previous-smaller.
approach: Keep a stack of indices whose heights increase from bottom to top.
When the incoming height is not larger, pop: the popped bar's rectangle spans from the element below it on the stack to the current index, exclusive at both ends.
Width is i - left - 1 where left is the new stack top (or -1 when the stack empties) — this handles the popped bar extending back past several taller bars.
Run one extra iteration with a virtual height of 0 to flush anything still on the stack.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — each index is pushed and popped once

prerequisites.label: Stack
prerequisites.why: Previous-smaller and next-smaller both fall out of one monotonic stack.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Widths are index arithmetic over a contiguous block.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree
problems.prompt: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth — the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
constraints: The tree is not necessarily balanced.
hints: Depth of a tree is defined in terms of the depth of its subtrees — that is a recurrence.
depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).
The base case is the null child, whose depth is 0.
approach: Recurse into both children and take the larger result.
Add one for the current node.
A null node returns 0, which terminates the recursion and makes leaves return 1.
This is a post-order DFS: both children are resolved before the node's own answer exists.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — every node is visited once
problems.spaceComplexity: O(h) for the call stack, where h is the height (O(n) if degenerate)

prerequisites.label: Tree
prerequisites.why: Node/child structure and the definition of height.

prerequisites.label: Depth-First Search (DFS)
prerequisites.why: Post-order recursion is DFS on a tree.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.prompt: Return the node values of a binary tree grouped level by level, from the root downwards.
constraints: Each inner list must contain exactly one level.
hints: Recursion goes deep first, which is the wrong order here — you need to finish a level before descending.
A queue gives you that: enqueue children as you dequeue parents.
To know where one level ends, snapshot the queue size before draining it.
approach: Seed a queue with the root (returning early on an empty tree).
Each round, read the current queue size — that count is exactly the current level's width.
Dequeue that many nodes into one list, enqueuing each node's non-null children behind them.
Repeat until the queue drains. The size snapshot is what separates levels.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(w) where w is the widest level

prerequisites.label: Queue
prerequisites.why: FIFO order is what produces level-by-level visiting.

prerequisites.label: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
prerequisites.why: This is textbook BFS with a level-size snapshot.

prerequisites.why: Children are enqueued through the node structure.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.prompt: Given a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count the islands. An island is land connected horizontally or vertically.

examples.note: The top-left blob and the bottom-right cell.

hints: A grid is a graph: each land cell is a node, edges join orthogonal land neighbours.
Counting islands is counting connected components — one traversal per unvisited component.
Sinking visited land to '0' as you go doubles as the visited-set, costing no extra memory.
approach: Scan every cell. Land that has not been consumed yet starts a new island — increment the count.
Flood that island with DFS (or BFS), flipping each visited cell to '0'.
The flood's bounds check plus the '1' test together stop recursion at edges and water.
Because each cell is flipped once, total work is proportional to the grid size regardless of island shapes.
problems.timeComplexity: O(rows × cols) — each cell is visited at most twice
problems.spaceComplexity: O(rows × cols) worst case for the recursion stack on an all-land grid

prerequisites.why: The flood fill is DFS over an implicit graph.

prerequisites.why: Connected components is the concept being counted.

prerequisites.why: The alternative solution unions adjacent land — useful contrast.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.prompt: You climb a staircase of n steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways can you reach the top?
constraints: Plain recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially.
hints: The last move onto step n came from step n-1 or step n-2, and nowhere else.
So ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) — Fibonacci wearing a costume.
Only two previous values are ever needed, so an array is unnecessary.
approach: Identify the state: ways(i) = number of distinct ways to stand on step i.
Write the recurrence from the last decision: arrive from i-1 with a 1-step, or from i-2 with a 2-step.
Base cases: ways(0) = ways(1) = 1.
Iterate upward carrying only the last two values, which collapses O(n) space to O(1).

prerequisites.label: Fibonacci (Dynamic Programming)
prerequisites.why: Same recurrence, same memo-then-roll optimisation.

prerequisites.label: Fibonacci
prerequisites.why: Seeing the exponential version first is what motivates DP.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.prompt: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. The array may be all negative.

examples.note: All negative — the best is the single largest element.

hints: Define the state as "best sum of a subarray ending exactly at index i" rather than "best overall so far".
At each index there are only two options: extend the previous best-ending-here, or start fresh at nums[i].
Track the global best separately — the running value can dip while the answer stays high.
approach: Seed both current and best with nums[0], which also handles the all-negative case.
For each later element, current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]) — the extend-or-restart decision.
Update best after every step.
Restarting is correct because a negative running sum can only hurt any subarray that extends through it.

prerequisites.label: Kadane's Algorithm
prerequisites.why: This problem is Kadane's algorithm, stated as an interview question.

prerequisites.label: Prefix Sum
prerequisites.why: The O(n²) prefix-difference solution is the baseline this improves on.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.prompt: Given house values along a street, take the largest total without ever taking two adjacent houses.
constraints: Greedy 'take every other house' is wrong — check [2, 1, 1, 2].
hints: At each house you have exactly two choices: take it, or skip it.
Taking house i forbids house i-1, so the total becomes nums[i] + best(i-2).
Skipping it leaves best(i-1). The answer is the larger — and only two prior values are needed.
approach: Define best(i) as the maximum take from the first i houses.
Recurrence: best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i]).
Carry two rolling variables instead of an array.
The empty prefix contributes 0, which handles the leading houses without special cases.

prerequisites.label: Fibonacci (Dynamic Programming)
prerequisites.why: Same two-term rolling-state shape, different recurrence.

prerequisites.label: 0/1 Knapsack
prerequisites.why: Take-or-skip with a constraint is the knapsack decision in miniature.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.prompt: Given coin denominations and an amount, return the fewest coins that make that amount, or -1 if it cannot be made.
constraints: Each coin may be used unlimited times.
hints: Greedy 'take the biggest coin' fails — try coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6.
Define dp[a] as the fewest coins making amount a, and think about the *last* coin used.
If the last coin is c, the rest is dp[a - c], so dp[a] = 1 + min over all usable c.
approach: Fill dp with an impossible sentinel (amount + 1) and set dp[0] = 0.
For each amount ascending, try every coin that fits and take the best dp[a - c] + 1.
Ascending order guarantees dp[a - c] is already final when it is read.
A remaining sentinel at dp[amount] means unreachable — return -1.

prerequisites.why: The topic covers this recurrence and the greedy counterexample.

prerequisites.why: This is the unbounded variant — same table, coins reusable.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.prompt: Given an array of distinct integers, return every possible subset (the power set), without duplicates.
hints: Every element is either in or out — that is a binary decision tree of depth n.
Every node of that tree is itself a valid subset, so record on entry rather than only at the leaves.
Pass a start index so each element is only ever considered after the ones before it, which prevents permuted duplicates.
approach: Maintain a mutable `path` holding the subset under construction.
On entering the recursion, snapshot `path` into the output — no separate base case is needed.
Loop i from `start`: append nums[i], recurse with i + 1, then remove the last element.
That removal is the backtrack — it restores the state for the next sibling branch.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the path and recursion depth, excluding output

prerequisites.label: Subset Sum
prerequisites.why: Same include/exclude tree, with a target test at the leaves.

prerequisites.label: Depth-First Search (DFS)
prerequisites.why: Backtracking is DFS over a decision tree with undo.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.prompt: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible orderings of its elements.
hints: Unlike subsets, order matters — so there is no start index; every unused element is a candidate at every depth.
Track which indices are already in the current path.
A complete path of length n is a finished permutation; that is the only place to record.
approach: Keep a `used` flag per index alongside the path being built.
At each level, try every unused index: mark used, append, recurse, then undo both.
Record only when the path reaches full length.
Undoing both the flag and the append is what makes sibling branches see a clean state.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n × n!) — n! permutations, each of length n
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the path, flags and recursion depth

prerequisites.label: Permutation Generation
prerequisites.why: The topic covers this exact recursion and its alternatives.

prerequisites.label: Depth-First Search (DFS)
prerequisites.why: The recursion tree is traversed depth-first with undo on the way back up.

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.prompt: Given distinct candidate numbers and a target, return every unique combination summing to the target. A candidate may be reused unlimited times.
constraints: All candidates are distinct positive integers.
Combinations are unordered — [2,3,3] and [3,2,3] are the same answer.
hints: Reuse is allowed, so recursing on the same index (not index + 1) keeps a candidate available.
Never going backwards past `start` is what stops [2,3,3] and [3,2,3] both appearing.
Carry the remaining target down instead of recomputing the path's sum at each node.
approach: Recurse with (start, remaining). Remaining hitting 0 means the path is a valid combination — record it.
For each candidate from `start` onwards, skip any that exceeds the remaining target.
Append it and recurse with the *same* index so it can be reused, and remaining - candidate.
Remove it on the way back out. Since all candidates are positive, remaining strictly decreases and the recursion terminates.
problems.timeComplexity: Exponential in target/min(candidate) — bounded by the number of valid combinations

prerequisites.label: Subset Sum
prerequisites.why: The bounded version of this search; compare the reuse rule.

prerequisites.label: Coin Change
prerequisites.why: Same structure counted with DP instead of enumerated — worth contrasting.

prerequisites.label: Depth-First Search (DFS)
prerequisites.why: Pruning on `remaining` is a depth-first search with early cutoff.

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.prompt: Given strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains any permutation of s1 as a contiguous substring.

examples.note: "boa" is not contiguous as a permutation.

hints: A permutation of s1 has exactly s1.length characters, so the window size never changes.
Two strings are permutations of each other exactly when their letter counts match.
Slide a fixed window over s2, adding the entering letter and removing the leaving one, and compare counts.
approach: Build a 26-slot count for s1 and an empty count for the window.
Extend the window one character at a time; once it exceeds s1.length, drop the character that fell off the left.
Compare the two count arrays after each step — equality means the window is a permutation.
Comparing 26 slots is O(1), so the whole scan stays linear.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — 26-slot comparison per step is constant

prerequisites.label: Sliding Window
prerequisites.why: Fixed-size window with an entering and a leaving element.

prerequisites.label: Counting Sort
prerequisites.why: The 26-slot tally is the counting idea used as a signature.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.prompt: Given a string and an integer k, you may replace at most k characters with any letter. Return the length of the longest substring of a single repeated letter you can produce.

examples.note: Replace both A's or both B's.
Replace the middle A to get "AABBBBA" → "BBBB".

hints: A window is achievable when the characters you must replace fit inside k.
That count is windowLength - (occurrences of the most frequent letter in the window).
The window only needs to shrink when that quantity exceeds k — and the answer never shrinks, so a single pass suffices.
approach: Track letter counts inside the window plus the highest count seen so far.
Extend the right edge, updating the count and the running max.
If windowLength - maxCount > k the window is unachievable — advance the left edge and drop its letter.
Record the window length after each step. The max count is deliberately never decreased: a stale max can only keep the window from shrinking, and a longer answer requires a genuinely higher count.

prerequisites.label: Sliding Window
prerequisites.why: A validity condition drives the shrink, not a fixed size.

prerequisites.label: Hash Table / Hash Map
prerequisites.why: Letter frequency inside the window is a count map.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.prompt: Given a string, decide whether it reads the same forwards and backwards, considering only alphanumeric characters and ignoring case.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

constraints: Solve without building a cleaned copy of the string.
hints: A palindrome is defined by pairs: first with last, second with second-last.
Walk two pointers inwards and compare as you go.
Skipping non-alphanumerics happens inside the loop, so no separate cleaning pass is needed.
approach: Start pointers at both ends.
Advance each past any non-alphanumeric character before comparing.
Compare lowercased characters; a mismatch ends it immediately.
Meeting in the middle without a mismatch means the string is a palindrome.

prerequisites.label: Two Pointer Technique
prerequisites.why: Converging pointers compare mirrored positions.

prerequisites.label: String
prerequisites.why: Character classification and case folding are string operations.

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.prompt: Given heights of vertical lines, pick two that together with the x-axis hold the most water. Return that maximum area.
constraints: Containers do not slant — area is min(left, right) × distance.
hints: Start with the widest possible container: the two ends.
Any move inwards loses width, so it can only help if it gains height.
Moving the taller line can never gain — the shorter one still caps the area. So move the shorter.
approach: Place pointers at both ends and compute the area each step.
Advance the pointer at the shorter line.
That discards every container using the shorter line, all of which are bounded by the area just measured.
Continue until the pointers meet, keeping the running maximum.

prerequisites.label: Two Pointer Technique
prerequisites.why: The greedy shrink argument is a two-pointer invariant.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Widths are index differences over a contiguous block.

problems.title: Middle of the Linked List
problems.prompt: Return the middle node of a singly linked list. With an even count, return the second of the two middle nodes.
constraints: Solve in one pass — no length counting first.
hints: Counting the length then walking half is two passes. Can one pointer's position encode another's?
If one pointer moves twice as fast, where is the slow one when the fast one finishes?
Exactly halfway — that is the entire solution.
approach: Start both pointers at the head.
Advance slow by one and fast by two each step.
Stop when fast or fast.next is null.
Slow now sits at the middle; the loop condition decides which middle an even-length list yields.

prerequisites.why: There is no index — position must be derived by walking.

problems.title: Happy Number
problems.prompt: Repeatedly replace a number by the sum of the squares of its digits. It is happy if this reaches 1; otherwise the process loops forever. Decide whether n is happy.

examples.note: Enters a cycle that never reaches 1.

constraints: Aim for O(1) extra space — no seen-set.
hints: The sequence is a chain of numbers where each has exactly one successor. What does 'loops forever' mean about that chain?
It has a cycle — so cycle detection applies, with digit-square-sum as the next() function.
Run fast/slow. They meet either at 1 (happy) or inside the unhappy cycle.
approach: Write next(x) as the sum of squares of x's digits.
Run slow one step and fast two steps per iteration.
Stop when fast reaches 1 or the two meet.
Meeting away from 1 means an unhappy cycle. A set of seen values also works but costs memory.
problems.timeComplexity: O(log n) per step, with a bounded number of steps

prerequisites.why: Floyd's detection over an implicit successor function.

problems.title: Non-Overlapping Intervals
problems.prompt: Given a set of intervals, return the minimum number you must remove so that the rest do not overlap.
constraints: Intervals touching at a boundary do not overlap: [1,2] and [2,3] are fine.
hints: Removing the fewest is the same as keeping the most — this is interval scheduling.
Sorting by *start* is wrong here; a long early interval blocks many later ones.
Sort by end time: always keeping the interval that finishes earliest leaves the most room for the rest.
approach: Sort by end time.
Keep the first interval and remember its end.
Take each subsequent interval whose start is ≥ that end, updating the end each time you take one.
The answer is total minus kept. The exchange argument proves earliest-finish is optimal.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep

prerequisites.why: Same greedy family: sort by a deadline-like key, then take what fits.

prerequisites.label: Merge Sort
prerequisites.why: Sorting by end time is the enabling step.

problems.title: Interval List Intersections
problems.prompt: Given two lists of pairwise-disjoint intervals, each sorted by start, return the intersection of the two lists.
constraints: Each list is sorted and internally disjoint.
hints: Both lists are sorted, so this is closer to merging two sorted lists than to interval merging.
For any pair, the intersection is [max of starts, min of ends] — and it is real only when that range is non-empty.
Advance the interval that ends first; it cannot intersect anything further along the other list.
approach: Keep an index into each list.
Compute lo = max(starts) and hi = min(ends) for the current pair; emit [lo, hi] when lo ≤ hi.
Advance the pointer whose interval has the smaller end.
Each step consumes one interval, so the sweep is linear in the combined size.

prerequisites.why: Two indices advance over two sorted sequences.

prerequisites.label: Merge Sort
prerequisites.why: The merge step's advance-the-smaller rule is reused verbatim.

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
problems.prompt: Given points on a plane and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin.
constraints: The answer may be returned in any order.
hints: Comparing distances never needs the square root — x² + y² preserves the ordering.
You want the k smallest, so the heap must evict the current worst: a max-heap of size k.
That is the mirror image of the kth-largest problem, which uses a min-heap.
approach: Order a heap by squared distance, descending, so its root is the farthest of those kept.
Push each point; whenever the heap exceeds k, poll the root.
After the pass the heap holds exactly the k nearest points.
Skipping the square root avoids floating point entirely.

prerequisites.why: A bounded max-heap selects the k smallest.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.prompt: Given CPU tasks labelled A–Z and a cooldown n, identical tasks must be separated by at least n intervals. Return the minimum total intervals, counting idles.

examples.note: A B idle A B idle A B.

hints: The schedule's length is dictated by the most frequent task — it defines the skeleton.
With max count m, that task creates m - 1 gaps, each of width n + 1 including the task itself.
Ties matter: every task sharing the max count adds one more slot to the final block.
approach: Count each task's frequency and find the maximum m and how many tasks tie at m.
The skeleton length is (m - 1) × (n + 1) + tiesAtMax.
If there are enough other tasks, they fill the idles instead of extending the schedule — so the answer is at least tasks.size.
Return the larger of the two. No simulation is needed.

problems.title: First and Last Position of an Element
problems.prompt: Given a sorted array with duplicates and a target, return the first and last index of the target, or [-1, -1] if absent.
constraints: The array is sorted ascending and may contain duplicates.
hints: Plain binary search returns *an* occurrence, not the first or last one.
On a hit, do not stop — record it and keep searching the side where an earlier (or later) copy would live.
Two runs of the same loop, differing only in which side is kept, give both bounds.
approach: Run the standard loop, but on equality record the index and continue instead of returning.
For the first position, continue leftwards by setting hi = mid - 1.
For the last position, continue rightwards by setting lo = mid + 1.
Each run stays O(log n), so the pair costs O(log n) overall.

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix
problems.prompt: Each row of a matrix is sorted ascending and each row's first value exceeds the previous row's last. Decide whether a target is present in O(log(m × n)).
constraints: The required runtime rules out searching row by row.
hints: Read the row conditions together: laid end to end, the whole matrix is one sorted sequence.
So binary search the range 0 until rows × cols as if it were a flat array.
Convert a flat index back with row = index / cols and column = index % cols.
approach: Treat indices 0 until rows × cols as a virtual sorted array.
Run the standard loop over that range.
Map each midpoint to a cell with integer division and modulo.
One search over m × n elements gives log(m × n) — no separate row search needed.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.prompt: Return an array where each position holds the product of every other element. Solve without division and in O(n).

examples.note: Zeroes are handled with no special case.

constraints: Division is not allowed — it breaks on zeroes.
O(1) extra space beyond the output array.
hints: The product excluding i is (everything left of i) × (everything right of i).
Those are prefix and suffix products — the multiplicative version of prefix sums.
Write the prefixes into the output on one pass, then multiply the suffixes in on a reverse pass.
approach: First pass, left to right: store the running product of everything before i into out[i].
Second pass, right to left: multiply out[i] by the running product of everything after i.
Both running products start at 1, which handles the ends without special cases.
The output array doubles as scratch space, so no extra arrays are allocated.

prerequisites.why: Prefix/suffix accumulation, with multiplication as the operator.

prerequisites.why: The output array is reused as scratch to hit O(1) space.

problems.title: Range Sum Query 2D
problems.prompt: Given a fixed matrix, answer many queries asking for the sum of a rectangular submatrix.
constraints: The matrix never changes after construction.
Up to 10⁴ queries — each must be O(1).
hints: Extend 1D prefix sums: prefix[r][c] = sum of the rectangle from the origin to (r, c).
Building it needs inclusion-exclusion — the two overlapping strips double-count their shared corner.
A query is the same idea in reverse: subtract the strip above and the strip left, then add back the corner.
approach: Allocate a (rows + 1) × (cols + 1) prefix grid so index 0 acts as a zero border.
Fill it with prefix[r+1][c+1] = value + prefix[r][c+1] + prefix[r+1][c] - prefix[r][c].
Answer a query as prefix[r2+1][c2+1] - prefix[r1][c2+1] - prefix[r2+1][c1] + prefix[r1][c1].
The final + prefix[r1][c1] restores the corner subtracted twice.
problems.timeComplexity: O(rows × cols) to build, O(1) per query

prerequisites.label: Prefix Sum
prerequisites.why: The 2D form is the same technique with inclusion-exclusion.

prerequisites.label: Array
prerequisites.why: Row-major layout and index offsets carry the zero border.

hints: Sorting both strings works but costs O(n log n).
Anagrams are defined by letter counts, so count instead of sort.
One pass can increment for one string and decrement for the other — all zeroes means anagram.
approach: Return false immediately on a length mismatch.
Walk both strings together, incrementing the count for s and decrementing for t.
Every slot ending at zero means each letter appeared equally often.
The fixed 26-slot array makes the space constant.

problems.title: Isomorphic Strings
problems.prompt: Two strings are isomorphic if the characters of one can be replaced to get the other, preserving order, with no two characters mapping to the same character.

examples.note: o would need to map to both a and r.

constraints: The mapping must be one-to-one in both directions.
hints: Record the mapping as you scan and check consistency at each position.
One map is not enough: "ab" → "aa" passes a forward-only check but is not isomorphic.
So also track which target characters are already claimed.
approach: Keep a forward map from s-characters to t-characters and a record of claimed t-characters.
At each index, if the s-character is unmapped, reject when its t-character is already claimed, otherwise record both.
If it is already mapped, reject on any disagreement with the current t-character.
Surviving the whole scan means the bijection is consistent.

problems.title: Min Stack
problems.prompt: Design a stack supporting push, pop, top and getMin, all in O(1).
constraints: All four operations must be O(1) — scanning for the minimum is not allowed.
pop, top and getMin are only called on a non-empty stack.
hints: One variable holding the minimum breaks on pop — you cannot recover the previous minimum.
Every element needs to remember what the minimum was while it was on top.
Push that alongside it, in a parallel stack.
approach: Keep two stacks: the values, and the minimum at each depth.
On push, push min(newValue, currentMin) onto the second stack.
On pop, pop both — the previous minimum is restored automatically.
getMin reads the top of the minimum stack, so every operation is O(1) at the cost of O(n) extra space.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the parallel minimum stack

prerequisites.why: The design is two stacks kept in lockstep.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.prompt: Evaluate an arithmetic expression in reverse Polish notation, where operators follow their operands.
hints: RPN needs no parentheses because the operand order is already fixed — what structure holds pending operands?
A stack: push numbers, and an operator consumes the two most recent.
Pop order matters — the first pop is the right operand.
approach: Scan the tokens left to right.
Push every number.
On an operator, pop twice; the first pop is the right-hand operand, the second the left.
Push the result back. The single value left at the end is the answer.

problems.title: Clone Graph
problems.prompt: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the whole graph.

examples.output: an identical 4-node graph of new objects

constraints: The graph is connected and undirected, so cycles are guaranteed.
hints: Undirected edges mean every edge is a 2-cycle — naive recursion never terminates.
Keep a map from original node to its copy and consult it before recursing.
Register a node's copy in the map *before* recursing into its neighbours, or a cycle re-enters and loops.
approach: Maintain a map from original to copy, which doubles as the visited-set.
On visiting a node, return its existing copy if present.
Otherwise create the copy, store it immediately, then recurse into each neighbour and attach the returned copies.
Register-before-recurse is what makes the cycle terminate.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(V) for the map and recursion

problems.prompt: Given a number of courses and prerequisite pairs [course, needs], decide whether every course can be completed.
hints: Model it as a directed graph: an edge from a prerequisite to the course that needs it.
Completing everything is possible exactly when the graph has no cycle — that is topological ordering.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a course whose remaining prerequisite count is zero.
approach: Build an adjacency list plus an in-degree count of unmet prerequisites per course.
Queue every course with in-degree zero.
Dequeue a course, count it as taken, and decrement its dependents; any that hits zero joins the queue.
If the taken count reaches numCourses, a full ordering exists. A shortfall means a cycle held some courses back.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(V + E) for the adjacency list and queue

problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.prompt: A robot starts at the top-left of an m × n grid and may move only right or down. How many distinct paths reach the bottom-right?
constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
hints: Every cell is entered from above or from the left, and nowhere else.
So paths(r, c) = paths(r-1, c) + paths(r, c-1), with the first row and column all 1.
Filling row by row means the previous row is all you need — one array suffices.
approach: State: paths(r, c) = number of ways to reach that cell.
Initialise a single row of 1s, representing the topmost row.
For each following row, sweep left to right adding the value to its left — the array then holds that row.
The last entry after m - 1 sweeps is the answer.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.prompt: Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence — characters in order but not necessarily contiguous.
constraints: Subsequence, not substring — gaps are allowed.
hints: Compare the last characters of the two prefixes you are considering.
If they match, both can be consumed together: 1 + LCS of the shorter prefixes.
If not, one of the two must be dropped — take the better of the two options.
approach: Define dp[i][j] as the LCS length of a's first i characters and b's first j.
Match → dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
Mismatch → dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Row and column 0 stay 0 (an empty string shares nothing), and the answer is the bottom-right cell.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(m × n), reducible to O(min(m, n)) with rolling rows

problems.prompt: Given digits 2–9, return every letter combination the number could spell on a phone keypad.
hints: Each digit contributes one character, so every result has exactly digits.length characters.
That makes the recursion depth fixed — one level per digit.
At each level, loop over that digit's letters, append, recurse, then remove.
approach: Map each digit to its letters.
Recurse on the digit index, carrying a partial string.
Reaching the end of the digits means the partial string is complete — record it.
Removing the appended character on the way out is the backtrack that lets siblings reuse the buffer.
problems.timeComplexity: O(4ⁿ × n) worst case, with n digits mapping to up to four letters

problems.prompt: Given a character grid and a word, decide whether the word can be spelled by walking to orthogonally adjacent cells without reusing a cell.

examples.note: The B would have to be reused.

constraints: A cell may not be used twice in one path.
hints: Try every cell as a starting point, then walk letter by letter.
"No reuse" needs a visited-marker — but only along the current path, not globally.
Overwrite the cell with a sentinel during the recursion and restore it afterwards; that restore is the backtrack.
approach: For each cell, launch a search matching word[0] onwards.
Fail fast when out of bounds or the character does not match; succeed when the whole word is consumed.
Mark the cell with a sentinel, recurse into all four neighbours, then restore the original character.
Restoring is essential — a different starting cell must see the grid untouched.
problems.timeComplexity: O(rows × cols × 4^L) worst case for a word of length L

problems.title: Reverse a Linked List
problems.prompt: Reverse a singly linked list in place and return the new head.
constraints: O(1) extra space — do not build a new list or an array.
hints: Each node's next must point at its predecessor instead of its successor.
Flipping a pointer destroys the only reference to the rest of the list — save it first.
Three references are enough: the node behind, the current node, and the one ahead.
approach: Start with prev = null and cur = head.
Save cur.next before overwriting it — this is the step everyone loses the list on.
Point cur.next at prev, then shift prev and cur forward by one.
When cur reaches null, prev is the new head.

prerequisites.why: Node/next mechanics and why order of assignment matters.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.prompt: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by splicing the existing nodes together.
constraints: Reuse the input nodes; do not allocate new ones.
hints: At each step the next output node is the smaller of the two current heads.
Appending needs a tail reference, and the first append has no tail yet.
A dummy head removes that special case — return dummy.next at the end.
approach: Create a dummy node and let tail track the end of the output.
While both lists have nodes, splice the smaller head on and advance that list.
When one list empties, attach the remainder of the other in one assignment — it is already sorted.
Return dummy.next, the real head.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(1) — nodes are spliced, not copied

prerequisites.label: Singly Linked List
prerequisites.why: Splicing means rewiring next, not copying values.

problems.title: Remove the Nth Node From the End
problems.prompt: Remove the nth node counting from the end of a singly linked list and return the head.
hints: Counting the length first is two passes. A fixed gap between two pointers encodes the same information.
Advance one pointer n + 1 steps first, then move both until the leader falls off the end.
The trailing pointer then sits just before the target — deleting needs the predecessor.
approach: Anchor both pointers at a dummy node placed before the head, so removing the first node needs no special case.
Advance the leader n + 1 steps.
Move both together until the leader is null; the trailer is now the target's predecessor.
Splice the target out with trailer.next = trailer.next.next and return dummy.next.

prerequisites.why: Deletion requires holding the predecessor.

problems.title: Palindrome Linked List
problems.prompt: Decide whether a singly linked list reads the same forwards and backwards, using O(1) extra space.
constraints: O(1) extra space — copying values into an array is not allowed.
hints: A singly linked list cannot be walked backwards — so make part of it point backwards.
Find the middle with fast/slow, then reverse the second half in place.
Compare the two halves in lockstep; unequal lengths simply stop when the reversed half ends.
approach: Locate the middle with the fast/slow walk.
Reverse the list from the middle onwards using the standard three-pointer loop.
Walk the original head and the reversed tail together, comparing values.
Stopping when the reversed half runs out handles odd lengths — the middle node is never compared against anything.
problems.spaceComplexity: O(1) — the second half is reversed in place

problems.title: Reorder List
problems.prompt: Reorder a list L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → … in place, without changing node values.
constraints: Only pointers may be modified — no value swapping.
hints: The output alternates between the front of the list and the back — but there is no way to walk backwards.
Split at the middle and reverse the second half; then "the back" becomes a forward walk.
Weave the two halves by alternately splicing one node from each.
approach: Find the middle with fast/slow and cut the list into two halves.
Reverse the second half in place.
Weave: repeatedly attach a node from the reversed half after the current front node, saving both successors first.
The loop ends when the reversed half is exhausted, which leaves the shorter first half correctly terminated.

problems.title: Invert a Binary Tree
problems.prompt: Mirror a binary tree: every node's left and right subtrees swap places.
constraints: Mirror the whole tree, not just the root's children.
hints: Swapping only the root's children is not enough — every level must mirror.
The mirror of a tree is a node whose left is the mirror of its right, and vice versa.
Capture one inverted subtree in a local before overwriting, or you will read back the value you just wrote.
approach: Return null for a null node — the base case.
Invert the left subtree and hold the result in a local variable.
Assign the inverted right subtree to left, then the saved value to right.
Ordering matters: assigning left first without saving loses the original left subtree.

prerequisites.why: Recursive structure: a node plus two subtrees.

problems.title: Diameter of a Binary Tree
problems.prompt: Return the length of the longest path between any two nodes, measured in edges. The path need not pass through the root.
hints: Any path has a single highest node — its turning point.
Through that node, the path length is leftDepth + rightDepth.
So compute depths recursively and, at every node, update a running best with that sum.
approach: Write a depth function returning 1 + max(left, right), with 0 for null.
Before returning, record left + right as a diameter candidate.
Track the maximum candidate across all nodes in an outer variable.
One post-order pass computes every depth and every candidate together — no repeated depth queries.
problems.timeComplexity: O(n) — each node's depth is computed once

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST
problems.prompt: Given a binary search tree and two values present in it, return their lowest common ancestor.

examples.note: A node can be its own ancestor.

constraints: Both values exist in the tree and are distinct.
The BST ordering invariant holds everywhere.
hints: In a general binary tree this needs a full search. The BST ordering gives you far more.
If both values are smaller than the current node, the answer must be in the left subtree — and symmetrically for larger.
The first node where they fall on opposite sides (or one equals the node) is the answer.
approach: Walk down from the root, no recursion required.
Both values below the node → go left. Both above → go right.
Anything else means the values split here, or one *is* here — that node is the LCA.
The walk is a single root-to-node descent, so it costs the tree's height.
problems.timeComplexity: O(h) — O(log n) on a balanced tree

prerequisites.why: The ordering invariant is what makes the descent decidable.

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.prompt: Decide whether a binary tree is a valid binary search tree: every node's whole left subtree is smaller and its whole right subtree larger.

examples.note: 4 sits in 5's right subtree but 3 is below 5.

constraints: Values are distinct; equality is not allowed on either side.
hints: Checking node.left.value < node.value < node.right.value locally is the classic wrong answer.
A node deep in a right subtree is still constrained by every ancestor it descended from.
Pass an allowed (low, high) range down and tighten it at each step.
approach: Recurse with an open interval that the node's value must lie strictly inside.
Going left tightens the upper bound to the current value; going right raises the lower bound.
A null node is vacuously valid.
Start with an unbounded range, using Long so that Int.MIN_VALUE and Int.MAX_VALUE nodes are handled.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.prompt: Return the kth smallest value in a binary search tree, counting from 1.
constraints: Stop as soon as the answer is known — do not flatten the whole tree.
hints: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in ascending order.
So the kth node visited in-order is the answer — no sorting needed.
Writing the traversal with an explicit stack lets you stop the moment the count reaches k.
approach: Push the leftmost spine onto a stack.
Pop a node — that is the next value in ascending order — and decrement the remaining count.
Hitting zero returns immediately, so the traversal short-circuits.
Otherwise descend into the popped node's right child and push its leftmost spine.
problems.timeComplexity: O(h + k) — only the visited prefix is traversed

problems.title: Assign Cookies
problems.prompt: Each child has a greed factor and each cookie a size. A child is content if their cookie is at least their greed. Maximise the number of content children.

examples.note: Only the least greedy child can be satisfied.

constraints: Each child receives at most one cookie.
hints: Giving a big cookie to a child a small one would satisfy is pure waste.
Sort both sides and match the least greedy child with the smallest cookie that works.
Every cookie is examined once, whether it is used or discarded.
approach: Sort greeds and cookies ascending.
Walk both with one index each. If the current cookie satisfies the current child, count it and advance the child.
Advance the cookie index either way — a cookie too small for the least greedy remaining child is useless to everyone else.
The exchange argument: swapping any matched pair for a smaller-cookie match never reduces the total.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.prompt: Each element is the maximum jump length from that position. Starting at index 0, decide whether the last index is reachable.

examples.note: Index 3 is a dead end that cannot be skipped.

hints: You do not need the *path*, only whether the end is reachable — so track reachability, not routes.
Sweep left to right maintaining the furthest index reachable so far.
Standing at an index beyond that furthest reach means the sweep hit an unbridgeable gap.
approach: Keep a single `reach` value, starting at 0.
At each index, fail immediately if the index exceeds `reach` — nothing can get here.
Otherwise extend `reach` to max(reach, i + nums[i]).
Surviving the whole sweep means the final index was always within reach. DP over every jump also works but costs O(n²).

Sweep with a running end that stretches to the furthest last-index seen so far; when the cursor reaches it, the part closes.
approach: First pass: record the last index of each letter.
Second pass: extend `end` to max(end, last[current letter]).
When the cursor equals `end`, every letter in the current part is fully contained — emit the length and start a new part.
Cutting at the earliest legal point is what maximises the number of parts.

If the tank goes negative somewhere between i and j, no start in that whole range can work.
So on failure, jump the candidate start past j entirely instead of retrying i + 1.
approach: Sweep once, accumulating both a total balance and a running tank of gas[i] - cost[i].
Whenever the tank drops below zero, reset it and move the candidate start to the next station.
The total balance decides feasibility: negative means no start works at all.
Otherwise the last candidate start is the answer — every station it skipped was proven impossible.

problems.title: Find the First Occurrence
problems.prompt: Return the index of the first occurrence of `needle` in `haystack`, or -1 if it is not present. Solve it in O(n + m) — the naive nested loop is O(n·m) and is not accepted.

examples.note: The later occurrence at index 6 is also a match, but the first one wins.
The case where naive matching wastes the most work.

hints: When a match breaks after j characters, those j characters are already known — the naive loop throws that knowledge away and rereads them.
Precompute, for each prefix of the needle, the longest proper prefix of it that is also a suffix. That number is how much of the match survives a mismatch.
With that table, the haystack pointer never has to move backwards: only the needle pointer falls back.
approach: Build the LPS table over the needle in O(m) — it is KMP run against itself.
Scan the haystack with i, tracking j = how many needle characters currently match.
On a mismatch with j > 0, set j = lps[j−1] and retry the same i; with j == 0, just advance i.
When j reaches m, the match started at i − m + 1.

problems.title: Built From a Repeated Block
problems.prompt: Given a string s, decide whether it can be constructed by taking some proper substring of it and concatenating that substring two or more times.

examples.note: "abc" four times — but "abcabc" twice also works.

constraints: Aim for O(n); trying every divisor length is O(n·√n) at best and O(n²) written naively.
hints: If s is a block repeated k times, then s overlaps itself when shifted by one block length.
The LPS table's last entry is the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix — call it L. The candidate block length is n − L.
s is periodic exactly when n − L divides n evenly and L > 0.
approach: Build the LPS table for s.
Let L = lps[n−1]; the smallest period is n − L.
Return L > 0 && n % (n − L) == 0.
The alternative trick — search for s inside (s + s) with the first and last characters removed — works for the same reason.

problems.prompt: Return the longest contiguous substring of s that reads the same forwards and backwards. Give the O(n²) centre-expansion solution first, then the linear one.

examples.note: "aba" is equally long and also accepted.
